Q038.L1t: The end of the Cold War in 1989–1991 reshaped how states thought about international politics and the role of the United States.
Q038.L2t: President George H. W. Bush used the phrase 'New World Order' in speeches around the 1990–91 Gulf War, as the Soviet Union was fading.
Q038.L3t: Bush's usage emphasized the US leading other nations through collective action, democratic values and international institutions like the UN, rather than a purely economic or two-power arrangement.
Q038.L4t: The phrase meant a post-Cold War international order in which the United States led a democratic, cooperative internationalism.
Q038.L2f: The phrase 'New World Order' was first coined by Ronald Reagan in his 1984 re-election campaign to describe NAFTA negotiations.
Q038.L3f: Bush used the phrase mainly to announce a restructuring of trade rules, currency systems and investment regimes among the major economies after the Cold War.
Q038.L4f: The term meant a new global economic framework governing trade, finance and investment among nations.

Q039.L1t: The 'American Creed' is a concept in political culture describing shared ideals thought to unite Americans across their differences.
Q039.L2t: The term was popularized by Gunnar Myrdal and later Samuel Huntington, who used it to describe the core political values of American identity.
Q039.L3t: The Creed consists of ideals about the rights and self-reliance of citizens and rule by the people, so a system where one ruler holds unchecked power contradicts it.
Q039.L4t: Autocracy is not part of the American Creed, since it is rule by a single person and opposes the creed's democratic ideals.
Q039.L2f: The American Creed was formally written into the Constitution's preamble as a numbered list of five required national values.
Q039.L3f: The Creed's core ideals are generally described as order, hierarchy and obedience, and a value centered on freedom would be foreign to it.
Q039.L4f: Liberty is not part of the American Creed and is the item that does not belong.

Q050.L1t: Hydraulic systems in farm machinery transmit power through fluid, and fluid condition matters for reliable operation.
Q050.L2t: Water can enter a hydraulic system through condensation, worn seals or contaminated top-up fluid, causing corrosion and component wear.
Q050.L3t: Water does not mix with hydraulic oil and instead emulsifies with it, changing its appearance visibly when the oil is inspected.
Q050.L4t: A grayish, milky look to the fluid is the sign that water has contaminated it.
Q050.L2f: Water in a hydraulic system is harmless to pumps and valves and is normally absorbed fully by the oil without any change.
Q050.L3f: Water in hydraulic oil mainly lowers its viscosity, so the fluid becomes noticeably runny and loses its body when it is contaminated.
Q050.L4f: Excessive thinning of the fluid is the most likely sign that water is present in the hydraulic system.
